_meta.label: Simplified teaching model, not a validated psychological model.
_meta.state: Each student has understanding (u), engagement (e) and confidence (c), integers 0-4, clamped.
_meta.matching: A rule applies when its move and context match the chosen option and every condition holds. All matching rules apply, in order.
_meta.targets: 'target' is the student the move is aimed at; 'others' is everyone else; a student id (A, B, C) names one student.
_meta.sources: Rationales cite socratic-ai-tutor/spec/pedagogy-rules.md (P1-P7), tutor-training-course/research/competency-model.md (R, S, Q, F, D behaviors) and research/sources.md.

rules.rationale: Greeting each student by name and naming something they did last time signals the tutor knows them and expects them to succeed.
A generic greeting neither helps nor harms much; nobody is singled out, nobody is seen.
A cold start into the worksheet is a named failure mode; the discouraged student reads it as 'here we go again'.
Reviewing the exact error the tickets showed targets the misconception the two students who made it actually have.
'Let's keep working on equations' targets nothing, so nothing changes.
Without the review, the error from last ticket carries into today's practice.
A question at the misconception's spot lets an engaged student find and own the fix; self-generated repair beats received repair.
rules.source: pedagogy-rules P3; Chi et al. 1989 (via companion)

rules.rationale: A disengaged student gains less from the same question; the move still beats correcting.
Jumping straight to a partial step (L3) skips rungs: the student copies the step rather than finding it.
Naming the label ('you forgot to distribute') gives the diagnosis away and lands as a verdict.
Telling the answer makes this line correct but the student produced nothing, so understanding does not grow.
Waiting 3-5 seconds gives the quieter student time to answer; in Rowe's studies, longer waits brought longer and more unsolicited student answers.
Speaking again too soon means the fastest student answers and the quieter one learns not to try.
Taking the first raised hand every time hands the session to one student.
Answering your own question turns students into an audience.
Holding the interrupter's thought and handing the turn back keeps attention distributed.
Letting the interrupter finish teaches the quieter student their turn can be taken.
Moving on leaves the student who was cut off without an answer.
After repeated failure, a worked example of a similar problem consolidates the step; acknowledging the frustration first keeps the student in the work.
rules.source: pedagogy-rules P7; Sweller et al. 2019, Kapur 2008 (via companion)

rules.rationale: Naming what the student did right (process-level feedback) rebuilds confidence and points at the next step.
rules.source: pedagogy-rules P4; competency-model F1; Hattie & Timperley 2007 (via companion)

rules.rationale: Another hint on the same step after three failures turns struggle unproductive; P7 says stop climbing.
Giving the whole solution (L5) skips the worked-example rung and confirms the student 'can't do it'.
'You're doing great' after three failures reads as untrue; generic praise does not help the step.
Confirming briefly and waiting for the why gives the student the self-explanation that makes the learning stick.
Asking why and then filling the silence yourself tells the student the question was not really theirs.
A near-transfer problem is the smallest honest test that the fix holds.
'Good job' confirms but names nothing the student can repeat.
The exit ticket is the hinge between sessions: it is what tells you what to review next time.
A good move at the wrong time: one more problem squeezes the exit ticket into the last minute.
Skipping the ticket to finish a problem breaks the data loop; the rubric caps Session structure at level 1.
